question: What primary component does the body manufacture during active immunity?
explanation: Active immunity relies on the body's own cells manufacturing specific antibodies to fight off identified foreign invaders. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h1)

question: Why does active immunity last much longer than passive immunity?

options.A: The liver stores extra white blood cells for decades
options.B: It relies entirely on proteins borrowed from another person
options.C: Foreign antibodies stay inside the bloodstream forever
options.D: The body creates its own permanent immune response records

explanation: When your own system builds the defense, it generates lasting immunological memory rather than relying on temporary borrowed antibodies. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h1)

question: What is the specific name for a foreign substance that triggers an immune response?
explanation: Antigens are the foreign markers on pathogens that the immune system recognizes as non-self and reacts against. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h2)

question: Why does a person often feel ill for a few days before starting to recover from a new infection?

options.A: It takes time for B-cells to build and release enough specific antibodies
options.B: White blood cells sleep for 72 hours before noticing any invasion
options.C: The body must wait for external antibodies to arrive from the liver
options.D: Pathogens immediately destroy all circulating red blood cells upon entry

explanation: The primary immune response requires a lag phase for recognition, activation, and antibody production before the pathogen can be cleared. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h2)

question: Which of the following is an example of natural active immunity?

options.A: Receiving a tetanus toxoid injection at the clinic
options.B: Getting a transfusion of maternal antibodies via breast milk
options.C: Recovering from a wild measles infection
options.D: Taking an intravenous course of broad-spectrum antibiotics

explanation: Natural active immunity develops when your body mounts its own defense after contracting an illness naturally in the environment. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h3)

question: What do natural active immunity and artificial active immunity have in common?

options.A: They both cause severe clinical disease before protection develops
options.B: They both provide only short-term protection lasting a few weeks
options.C: They both require a direct injection given by a healthcare worker
options.D: They both stimulate the body to produce its own lasting antibodies

explanation: Regardless of whether the antigen enters via illness or a vaccine, the internal immune response and resulting memory production are identical. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h3)

question: What is the primary function of memory cells in the immune system?

options.A: To recognize and respond rapidly to future repeat infections
options.B: To filter waste products directly out of the lymphatic fluid
options.C: To produce extra red blood cells during heavy blood loss
options.D: To digest dead cellular debris left over from tissue injury

explanation: Memory cells persist long-term to provide a fast, powerful defense if the same pathogen invades the body a second time. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h4)

question: How does the secondary immune response differ from the primary response when a pathogen returns?

options.A: It is much faster and produces a larger amount of antibodies immediately
options.B: It causes much worse symptoms before clearing the microbe
options.C: It relies entirely on borrowed antibodies from the mother's circulation
options.D: It takes twice as long to recognize the foreign antigen markers

explanation: Because memory cells are already waiting, the secondary response skips the delay and overwhelms the pathogen before illness starts. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h4)

question: What is the main purpose of giving a vaccine to an infant?

options.A: To replace the need for exclusive breastfeeding during the first year
options.B: To stimulate artificial active immunity safely without causing disease
options.C: To provide immediate temporary antibodies that last for one week
options.D: To destroy all normal gut flora to prevent future tummy aches

explanation: Vaccines safely train the infant immune system to recognize dangerous pathogens and build long-term memory cells. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h5)

question: A mother is worried because her baby developed a mild fever and slight thigh swelling after routine immunizations. What is the most appropriate midwifery response?

options.A: Tell her that vaccines should never be given again because of these dangerous signs
options.B: Advise her to immediately bring the child back for a full course of potent antibiotics
options.C: Explain that the vaccine formula was spoiled by improper storage in the clinic
options.D: Reassure her that this normal reaction shows the immune system is responding to the vaccine

explanation: Mild local soreness and low fever are common, expected signs that the immune system is actively reacting to the vaccine antigens. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of active immunity?

options.A: It can be stimulated safely through routine vaccination
options.B: It provides only temporary protection lasting for just a few weeks
options.C: It generates long-lived memory cells for future defense
options.D: It involves the person's own white blood cells producing antibodies

explanation: Active immunity lasts for years or a lifetime, whereas short-lived protection lasting a few weeks is a defining feature of passive immunity. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h6)

question: Why does an infant depend on passive immunity during the first few months of life?

options.A: Active immunity is completely impossible until a child reaches school age
options.B: Breast milk permanently stops the infant's own bone marrow from ever making blood cells
options.C: The infant's immune system is immature and cannot yet build fast active responses to all exposures
options.D: Maternal antibodies block vaccines from working for the first ten years of life

explanation: Babies rely on borrowed maternal antibodies to bridge the gap while their own immune system develops the capacity for robust active responses. [learn more](BMP111_U6_T7#BMP111_U6_T7_h6)
